46	# If True, exceptions include the doc content in the error message.

51	def set_pointer(doc, pointer, value, inplace=True):
52	    """Resolves a pointer against doc and sets the value of the target within doc.
53	
54	    With inplace set to true, doc is modified as long as pointer is not the
55	    root.
56	
57	    >>> obj = {'foo': {'anArray': [ {'prop': 44}], 'another prop': {'baz': 'A string' }}}
58	
59	    >>> set_pointer(obj, '/foo/anArray/0/prop', 55) == \
60	    {'foo': {'another prop': {'baz': 'A string'}, 'anArray': [{'prop': 55}]}}
61	    True
62	
63	    >>> set_pointer(obj, '/foo/yet another prop', 'added prop') == \
64	    {'foo': {'another prop': {'baz': 'A string'}, 'yet another prop': 'added prop', 'anArray': [{'prop': 55}]}}
65	    True
66	
67	    >>> obj = {'foo': {}}
68	    >>> set_pointer(obj, '/foo/a%20b', 'x') == \
69	    {'foo': {'a%20b': 'x' }}
70	    True
71	    """
72	
73	    pointer = JsonPointer(pointer)
74	    return pointer.set(doc, value, inplace)

77	def resolve_pointer(doc, pointer, default=_nothing):
78	    """ Resolves pointer against doc and returns the referenced object
79	
80	    >>> obj = {'foo': {'anArray': [ {'prop': 44}], 'another prop': {'baz': 'A string' }}, 'a%20b': 1, 'c d': 2}
81	
82	    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '') == obj
83	    True
84	
85	    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/foo') == obj['foo']
86	    True
87	
88	    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/foo/another prop') == obj['foo']['another prop']
89	    True
90	
91	    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/foo/another prop/baz') == obj['foo']['another prop']['baz']
92	    True
93	
94	    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/foo/anArray/0') == obj['foo']['anArray'][0]
95	    True
96	
97	    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/some/path', None) == None
98	    True
99	
100	    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/a b', None) == None
101	    True
102	
103	    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/a%20b') == 1
104	    True
105	
106	    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/c d') == 2
107	    True
108	
109	    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/c%20d', None) == None
110	    True
111	    """

113	    pointer = JsonPointer(pointer)
114	    return pointer.resolve(doc, default)

117	def pairwise(iterable):
118	    """ Transforms a list to a list of tuples of adjacent items
119	
120	    s -> (s0,s1), (s1,s2), (s2, s3), ...
121	
122	    >>> list(pairwise([]))
123	    []
124	
125	    >>> list(pairwise([1]))
126	    []
127	
128	    >>> list(pairwise([1, 2, 3, 4]))
129	    [(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]
130	    """
131	    a, b = tee(iterable)
132	    for _ in b:
133	        break
134	    return zip(a, b)
135

137	class JsonPointerException(Exception):
138	    pass
139	
140	
141	class EndOfList:
142	    """Result of accessing element "-" of a list"""
143	
144	    def __init__(self, list_):
145	        self.list_ = list_
146	
147	    def __repr__(self):
148	        return '{cls}({lst})'.format(cls=self.__class__.__name__,
149	                                     lst=repr(self.list_))
150	
151	
152	class JsonPointer:
153	    """A JSON Pointer that can reference parts of a JSON document"""
154	
155	    # Array indices must not contain:
156	    # leading zeros, signs, spaces, decimals, etc
157	    _RE_ARRAY_INDEX = re.compile('0|[1-9][0-9]*$')
158	    _RE_INVALID_ESCAPE = re.compile('(~[^01]|~$)')
159	
160	    def __init__(self, pointer):
161	
162	        # validate escapes
163	        invalid_escape = self._RE_INVALID_ESCAPE.search(pointer)
164	        if invalid_escape:
165	            raise JsonPointerException('Found invalid escape {}'.format(
166	                invalid_escape.group()))
167	
168	        parts = pointer.split('/')
169	        if parts.pop(0) != '':
170	            raise JsonPointerException('Location must start with /')
171	
172	        parts = [unescape(part) for part in parts]
173	        self.parts = parts
174	
175	    def to_last(self, doc):
176	        """Resolves ptr until the last step, returns (sub-doc, last-step)"""
177	
178	        if not self.parts:
179	            return doc, None
180	
181	        for part in self.parts[:-1]:
182	            doc = self.walk(doc, part)
183	
184	        return doc, JsonPointer.get_part(doc, self.parts[-1])
185	
186	    def resolve(self, doc, default=_nothing):
187	        """Resolves the pointer against doc and returns the referenced object"""
188	
189	        for part in self.parts:
190	
191	            try:
192	                doc = self.walk(doc, part)
193	            except JsonPointerException:
194	                if default is _nothing:
195	                    raise
196	                else:
197	                    return default
198	
199	        return doc
200	
201	    get = resolve
202	
203	    def set(self, doc, value, inplace=True):
204	        """Resolve the pointer against the doc and replace the target with value."""
205	
206	        if len(self.parts) == 0:
207	            if inplace:
208	                raise JsonPointerException('Cannot set root in place')
209	            return value
210	
211	        if not inplace:
212	            doc = copy.deepcopy(doc)
213	
214	        (parent, part) = self.to_last(doc)
215	
216	        if isinstance(parent, str):
217	            raise JsonPointerException("Cannot set value in a string")
218	        elif isinstance(parent, Sequence) and part == '-':
219	            parent.append(value)
220	        else:
221	            try:
222	                parent[part] = value
223	            except (TypeError, IndexError) as e:
224	                raise JsonPointerException("Invalid assignment target: %s" % (e,))
225	
226	        return doc
227	
228	    @classmethod
229	    def get_part(cls, doc, part):
230	        """Returns the next step in the correct type"""
231	
232	        if isinstance(doc, Mapping):
233	            return part
234	
235	        elif isinstance(doc, str):
236	            raise JsonPointerException("Cannot apply token '%s' to non-container type %s" % (part, type(doc)))
237	
238	        elif isinstance(doc, Sequence):
239	
240	            if part == '-':
241	                return part
242	
243	            if not JsonPointer._RE_ARRAY_INDEX.fullmatch(str(part)):
244	                raise JsonPointerException("'%s' is not a valid sequence index" % part)
245	
246	            try:
247	                return int(part)
248	            except ValueError as e:
249	                raise JsonPointerException("Invalid sequence index: %s" % (e,))
250	
251	        elif hasattr(doc, '__getitem__'):
252	            # Allow indexing via ducktyping
253	            # if the target has defined __getitem__
254	            return part
255	
256	        else:
257	            raise JsonPointerException("Document '%s' does not support indexing, "
258	                                       "must be mapping/sequence or support __getitem__" % type(doc))
259	
260	    def get_parts(self):
261	        """Returns the list of the parts. For example, JsonPointer('/a/b').get_parts() == ['a', 'b']"""
262	
263	        return self.parts
264	
265	    def walk(self, doc, part):
266	        """ Walks one step in doc and returns the referenced part """
267	
268	        part = JsonPointer.get_part(doc, part)
269	
270	        assert hasattr(doc, '__getitem__'), "invalid document type %s" % (type(doc),)
271	
272	        if isinstance(doc, Sequence):
273	            if part == '-':
274	                return EndOfList(doc)
275	
276	            try:
277	                return doc[part]
278	
279	            except IndexError:
280	                raise JsonPointerException("index '%s' is out of bounds" % (part,))
281	
282	        # Else the object is a mapping or supports __getitem__(so assume custom indexing)
283	        try:
284	            return doc[part]
285	
286	        except KeyError:
287	            if VERBOSE_EXCEPTIONS:
288	                raise JsonPointerException("member '%s' not found in %s" % (part, doc))
289	            else:
290	                raise JsonPointerException("member '%s' not found" % (part,))
291	
292	    def contains(self, ptr):
293	        """ Returns True if self contains the given ptr """
294	        return self.parts[:len(ptr.parts)] == ptr.parts
295	
296	    def __contains__(self, item):
297	        """ Returns True if self contains the given ptr """
298	        return self.contains(item)
299	
300	    def join(self, suffix):
301	        """ Returns a new JsonPointer with the given suffix append to this ptr """
302	        if isinstance(suffix, JsonPointer):
303	            suffix_parts = suffix.parts
304	        elif isinstance(suffix, str):
305	            suffix_parts = JsonPointer(suffix).parts
306	        else:
307	            suffix_parts = suffix
308	        try:
309	            return self.__class__.from_parts(chain(self.parts, suffix_parts))
310	        except:  # noqa E722
311	            raise JsonPointerException("Invalid suffix")
312	
313	    def __truediv__(self, suffix):
314	        return self.join(suffix)
315	
316	    @property
317	    def path(self):
318	        """Returns the string representation of the pointer
319	
320	        >>> ptr = JsonPointer('/~0/0/~1').path == '/~0/0/~1'
321	        """
322	        parts = [escape(part) for part in self.parts]
323	        return ''.join('/' + part for part in parts)
324	
325	    def __eq__(self, other):
326	        """Compares a pointer to another object
327	
328	        Pointers can be compared by comparing their strings (or splitted
329	        strings), because no two different parts can point to the same
330	        structure in an object (eg no different number representations)
331	        """
332	
333	        if not isinstance(other, JsonPointer):
334	            return False
335	
336	        return self.parts == other.parts
337	
338	    def __hash__(self):
339	        return hash(tuple(self.parts))
340	
341	    def __str__(self):
342	        return self.path
343	
344	    def __repr__(self):
345	        return type(self).__name__ + "(" + repr(self.path) + ")"
346	
347	    @classmethod
348	    def from_parts(cls, parts):
349	        """Constructs a JsonPointer from a list of (unescaped) paths
350	
351	        >>> JsonPointer.from_parts(['a', '~', '/', 0]).path == '/a/~0/~1/0'
352	        True
353	        """
354	        parts = [escape(str(part)) for part in parts]
355	        ptr = cls(''.join('/' + part for part in parts))
356	        return ptr
357	
358	
359	def escape(s):
360	    return s.replace('~', '~0').replace('/', '~1')
361	
362	
363	def unescape(s):
364	    return s.replace('~1', '/').replace('~0', '~')

python-json-pointer
===================

[![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/jsonpointer.svg)](https://pypi.python.org/pypi/jsonpointer/)

[![Coverage Status](https://coveralls.io/repos/github/stefankoegl/python-json-pointer/badge.svg?branch=master)](https://coveralls.io/github/stefankoegl/python-json-pointer?branch=master)


Resolve JSON Pointers in Python
-------------------------------

Library to resolve JSON Pointers according to
[RFC 6901](http://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6901)

See source code for examples
* Website: https://github.com/stefankoegl/python-json-pointer
* Repository: https://github.com/stefankoegl/python-json-pointer.git
* Documentation: https://python-json-pointer.readthedocs.org/
* PyPI: https://pypi.python.org/pypi/jsonpointer
* GitHub Actions: https://github.com/stefankoegl/python-json-pointer/actions
* Coveralls: https://coveralls.io/github/stefankoegl/python-json-pointer
Tutorial
========

Please refer to `RFC 6901 <http://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6901>`_ for the exact
pointer syntax. ``jsonpointer`` has two interfaces. The ``resolve_pointer``
method is basically a deep ``get``.

.. code-block:: python

    >>> from jsonpointer import resolve_pointer
    >>> obj = {"foo": {"anArray": [ {"prop": 44}], "another prop": {"baz": "A string" }}}

    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '') == obj
    True

    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/foo') == obj['foo']
    True

    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/foo/another prop') == obj['foo']['another prop']
    True

    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/foo/another prop/baz') == obj['foo']['another prop']['baz']
    True

    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/foo/anArray/0') == obj['foo']['anArray'][0]
    True

    >>> resolve_pointer(obj, '/some/path', None) == None
    True


The ``set_pointer`` method allows modifying a portion of an object using
JSON pointer notation:

.. code-block:: python

    >>> from jsonpointer import set_pointer
    >>> obj = {"foo": {"anArray": [ {"prop": 44}], "another prop": {"baz": "A string" }}}

    >>> set_pointer(obj, '/foo/anArray/0/prop', 55)
    {'foo': {'another prop': {'baz': 'A string'}, 'anArray': [{'prop': 55}]}}

    >>> obj
    {'foo': {'another prop': {'baz': 'A string'}, 'anArray': [{'prop': 55}]}}

By default ``set_pointer`` modifies the original object.  Pass ``inplace=False``
to create a copy and modify the copy instead:

    >>> from jsonpointer import set_pointer
    >>> obj = {"foo": {"anArray": [ {"prop": 44}], "another prop": {"baz": "A string" }}}

    >>> set_pointer(obj, '/foo/anArray/0/prop', 55, inplace=False)
    {'foo': {'another prop': {'baz': 'A string'}, 'anArray': [{'prop': 55}]}}

    >>> obj
    {'foo': {'another prop': {'baz': 'A string'}, 'anArray': [{'prop': 44}]}}

The ``JsonPointer`` class wraps a (string) path and can be used to access the
same path on several objects.

.. code-block:: python

    >>> import jsonpointer

    >>> pointer = jsonpointer.JsonPointer('/foo/1')

    >>> obj1 = {'foo': ['a', 'b', 'c']}
    >>> pointer.resolve(obj1)
    'b'

    >>> obj2 = {'foo': {'0': 1, '1': 10, '2': 100}}
    >>> pointer.resolve(obj2)
    10
The ``jsonpointer`` commandline utility
=======================================

The JSON pointer package also installs a ``jsonpointer`` commandline utility
that can be used to resolve a JSON pointers on JSON files.

The program has the following usage ::

    usage: jsonpointer [-h] [-f POINTER_FILE | -p POINTER] [--indent INDENT] [-v]
                       [POINTER] FILE [FILE ...]

    Resolve a JSON pointer on JSON files

    positional arguments:
      POINTER               A JSON pointer expression (if neither -f nor -p is
                            given)
      FILE                  Files for which the pointer should be resolved

    options:
      -h, --help            show this help message and exit
      -f POINTER_FILE, --pointer-file POINTER_FILE
                            File containing a JSON pointer expression
      -p POINTER, --pointer POINTER
                            A JSON pointer expression
      --indent INDENT       Indent output by n spaces
      -v, --version         show program's version number and exit

The pointer can be passed as the first positional argument, with ``-p``, or
read from a file with ``-f``.

The exit status is 0 if the pointer could be resolved on all files, 1 if it
could not be resolved on at least one file (the remaining files are still
processed) and 2 on usage errors, such as an invalid pointer or a missing
file.

Example
^^^^^^^

.. code-block:: bash

    # inspect JSON files
    $ cat a.json
    { "a": [1, 2, 3] }

    $ cat b.json
    { "a": {"b": [1, 3, 4]}, "b": 1 }

    # resolve JSON pointer
    $ jsonpointer /a a.json b.json
    [1, 2, 3]
    {"b": [1, 3, 4]}

    # same, using the -p option
    $ jsonpointer -p /a a.json b.json
    [1, 2, 3]
    {"b": [1, 3, 4]}

    # same, reading the pointer from a file
    $ cat ptr.txt
    /a

    $ jsonpointer -f ptr.txt a.json b.json
    [1, 2, 3]
    {"b": [1, 3, 4]}

#!/usr/bin/env python3


import argparse
import json
import sys

import jsonpointer

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
    description='Resolve a JSON pointer on JSON files')

# Accept pointer as option, as file or as first positional argument
ptr_group = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group()

ptr_group.add_argument('-f', '--pointer-file', type=argparse.FileType('r'),
                       help='File containing a JSON pointer expression')

ptr_group.add_argument('-p', '--pointer', type=str,
                       help='A JSON pointer expression')

parser.add_argument('POINTER', type=str, nargs='?',
                    help='A JSON pointer expression (if neither -f nor -p '
                         'is given)')

parser.add_argument('FILE', type=str, nargs='+',
                    help='Files for which the pointer should be resolved')
parser.add_argument('--indent', type=int, default=None,
                    help='Indent output by n spaces')
parser.add_argument('-v', '--version', action='version',
                    version='%(prog)s ' + jsonpointer.__version__)


def main():
    try:
        ok = resolve_files()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        sys.exit(1)

    if not ok:
        sys.exit(1)


def parse_pointer(args):
    """ Return the pointer and the list of files to resolve it on

    If the pointer is given via -f or -p, a POINTER positional argument is
    actually the first file. """
    files = args.FILE

    if args.pointer is not None or args.pointer_file is not None:
        if args.POINTER is not None:
            files = [args.POINTER] + files

        if args.pointer is not None:
            ptr = args.pointer
        else:
            # 2026-10-11: Trim file line endings without changing member names.
            ptr = args.pointer_file.read().rstrip("\r\n")

    elif args.POINTER is not None:
        ptr = args.POINTER

    else:
        parser.error('a JSON pointer is required (POINTER, -p or -f)')

    # Catches e.g. `jsonpointer a.json b.json`, where the pointer was omitted
    # and the first file would otherwise be used as the pointer
    try:
        jsonpointer.JsonPointer(ptr)
    except jsonpointer.JsonPointerException as e:
        parser.error('invalid JSON pointer %r: %s' % (ptr, e))

    return ptr, files


def resolve_files():
    """ Resolve a JSON pointer on JSON files

    Returns False if the pointer could not be resolved on at least one
    file. """
    args = parser.parse_args()

    ptr, files = parse_pointer(args)
    ok = True

    for name in files:
        try:
            f = argparse.FileType('r')(name)
        except argparse.ArgumentTypeError as e:
            parser.error(str(e))

        doc = json.load(f)
        try:
            result = jsonpointer.resolve_pointer(doc, ptr)
            print(json.dumps(result, indent=args.indent))
        except jsonpointer.JsonPointerException as e:
            print('Could not resolve pointer: %s' % str(e), file=sys.stderr)
            ok = False

    return ok


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

== resolve-set I did not probe the CLI (bin/jsonpointer), join, contains, or eq/hash, which belong to other areas. I did not fuzz against a reference implementation, so I covered about 12 hand-picked edge-case groups in resolve, set, walk, get_part and to_last. I did not test non-str pointer inputs beyond JsonPointer(None), which raises TypeError. That is outside documented behaviour. I did not test VERBOSE_EXCEPTIONS=False behaviour. Mutable Sequence types other than list (such as bytearray or deque) were not exercised.
- rejected | Array index grammar (leading zeros, signs, unicode digits, empty, '-', negative, out of range, huge) in resolve/get_part/to_last
- rejected | Escape decoding order (~01, ~001, ~00, a~01b, ~0~1) and empty-string keys
- ambiguity | set_pointer with '-' on a tuple parent raises AttributeError instead of JsonPointerException
   repro: set_pointer({'a':(1,2)}, '/a/-', 3)   # compare: set_pointer({'a':(1,2)}, '/a/0', 3) 
   exp: Probably JsonPointerException, consistent with the '/a/0' case, but the docs are silent for non-JSON immutable sequences. 
   act: '/a/-' raises AttributeError: 'tuple' object has no attribute 'append'. '/a/0' raises JsonPointerException 'Invalid assignment target'. The library's own error type is therefore inconsistent for a non-JSON input.
- rejected | set_pointer inplace semantics (root, return value, deepcopy, failure leaves original untouched, '-' append)
- rejected | doc/tutorial.rst doctest output differs in dict key order
- rejected | resolve default argument semantics and error types
- ambiguity | Custom __getitem__ object raising IndexError is not mapped to JsonPointerException (default not honoured)
   repro: class C:
    def __getitem__(self,k): raise IndexError(k)
resolve_pointer(C(), '/x', 'D') 
   exp: Unclear. The docs say nothing about __getitem__ objects that raise other exceptions. A reader could expect 'D' or JsonPointerException. 
   act: IndexError propagates out of resolve_pointer even with a default supplied. This is only reachable with non-JSON ducktyped containers, and the documented ducktyping tests use KeyError only.
- rejected | to_last / get_part / EndOfList traversal and set via '/-' mid-path
== class-api About 12 probes plus exhaustive small-alphabet enumeration. Not covered: resolve/set (another area), the CLI, non-str inputs such as bytes passed to __init__ (they raise TypeError, which is undocumented), and Sequence-like custom classes. I found no reproducible bug in the JsonPointer class API.
- rejected | Pointer validity, path round-trip, from_parts and hash vs RFC 6901 grammar
- rejected | Module doctests (path, from_parts, pairwise, resolve_pointer, set_pointer)
- rejected | join / __truediv__ with str, JsonPointer and list suffixes
- rejected | contains / __contains__ direction and boundary cases
- ambiguity | contains / 'in' with a str argument raises AttributeError
   repro: p=JsonPointer('/a/b/c'); p.contains('/a'); '/a' in p 
   exp: Undocumented. A reader might expect str to be accepted, as in join, or a JsonPointerException. 
   act: AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'parts'
- ambiguity | Fragment form '#/a' is not accepted
   repro: JsonPointer('#/a'); JsonPointer('#') 
   exp: RFC section 6 describes a URI fragment form. The library documents only the string form and never claims fragment support. 
   act: JsonPointerException: Location must start with /. This is consistent with the documented string representation, and percent-decoding is explicitly not done.
- ambiguity | get_parts() returns the internal list, so mutating it changes the pointer
   repro: q=JsonPointer('/a/b'); q.get_parts().append('z'); q.path 
   exp: Unspecified. Pointers are hashable, so a mutable view could change hash and equality. 
   act: '/a/b/z' (the pointer was mutated)
- ambiguity | join with a bytes suffix yields numeric parts
   repro: JsonPointer('/a/b/c').join(b'/a') 
   exp: Undocumented. Either an error or a bytes-based interpretation is plausible. 
   act: JsonPointer('/a/b/c/47/97'), because iterating bytes yields ints that are then stringified.
- rejected | __eq__, __hash__, set membership, subclass and repr behaviour
- rejected | from_parts edge inputs
== cli I ran with plain `python3` and PYTHONPATH, not `-I`, because `-I` ignores PYTHONPATH and makes `import jsonpointer` fail. I did not test Windows line endings through real stdin pipes for -f. I did not test very large files or special files such as FIFOs. I did not check --help output text against the docs usage block byte for byte. The library's own resolution behaviour (non-CLI) was out of scope.

   exp: 'Could not resolve pointer: ...' on stderr for each file, exit 1, with the second file still processed. This matches the RFC's error condition and the same handling as other unresolvable pointers. 
   act: Python traceback ending in 'TypeError: Object of type EndOfList is not JSON serializable' and exit status 1. The library's resolve_pointer returns an EndOfList object for '-', and json.dumps in bin/jsonpointer line 96 is outside the try that catches JsonPointerException. The second file is never processed. Run with only one file, /a/- gives the same traceback. See scratch/cli/probe.sh.
- ambiguity | Invalid JSON or non-UTF-8 input file yields a traceback and exit 1, and later files are not processed
   repro: printf notjson > bad.json; printf '\xff' > badenc.json; python3 <workspace>/bin/jsonpointer /a bad.json a.json; python3 <workspace>/bin/jsonpointer /a badenc.json a.json 
   exp: Undocumented. It could reasonably be a clean error with exit 2 (like a missing file) or exit 1 with the remaining files processed. 
   act: Uncaught json.JSONDecodeError or UnicodeDecodeError traceback, exit 1. The remaining files are not processed.
- ambiguity | A pointer file cannot address a member name ending in a newline (all trailing CR/LF are stripped)
   repro: printf '{"a\\n":"newline member","a":"plain"}' > nlm.json; printf '/a\n\n' > nl3.txt; python3 <workspace>/bin/jsonpointer -f nl3.txt nlm.json; python3 <workspace>/bin/jsonpointer -p "$(printf '/a\n')" nlm.json 
   exp: Unclear. A pointer file that ends in '/a' plus two newlines could mean member 'a\n', but the docs do not say how many line endings are trimmed. 
   act: Both print "plain" (member 'a'). rstrip('\r\n') removes every trailing CR/LF, so a member name ending in a newline cannot be addressed via -f. Using -p with $(...) also strips the newline, but that comes from the shell.
- ambiguity | --indent 0 and negative values still insert newlines

   exp: The docs do not define 0 or negative values. Without --indent the output is compact. 
   act: Both print '[\n1,\n2,\n3\n]'. This is Python json.dumps semantics for indent=0 and negative indent, not a clear contradiction.
- rejected | Exit-status contract, argument handling and special characters behave as documented
